newsitem.title: UK: Red hot UK data reignite rate rise fears.
newsitem.headline: Red hot UK data reignite rate rise fears.

text.p: By Cheryl Juckes,

A post-election UK rate rise might need to be as large as 50 basis points to keep inflation under control after a sizzling set of labour market and retail sales data released on Wednesday, analysts said.
"We will see 50 basis points on UK interest rates within a few months of the general election," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell UK economist Ciaran Barr.
"It may come in two parts but you can't rule out a single 1/2 point rise. It's all contingent on the Bank of England," he said.
"Even if you extrapolate out all of the funnies, we're still seeing pretty strong growth in the economy," he said.

UK average earnings data leapt up to 5.0 percent in January -- possibly distorted upwards by financial sector bonus payments -- whilst retail sales for February were up an annual 4.4 percent, compared with expectations of just 3.6 percent growth.

On the London International Financial Futures Exchange, June short sterling tumbled 10 basis points to 93.40, more than discounting a 50 basis point rate rise, whilst further out the losses were even more dramatic with the June 1998 contract now almost discounting rates at 7.40 percent.
Gardiner said the data confirmed the UK economy was tightening significantly, keeping upward pressure on wage inflation.
He argues that Bank of England Governor Eddie George has in fact been far too cautious in his demands for a rate rise of just 1/4 point.

"I think history will eventually show that Bank of England Governor Eddie George may have put the decimal point in the wrong place," he said -- suggesting a 2.5 point rate rise was needed rather than 0.25 point.

The minutes of the February 5 monthly monetary meeting showed that the Bank has retreated from a former warning that rates might need to rise by 0.5 point and is stressing the need for a rise of 0.25 point.

But Royal Bank of Scotland economist Marion Bell said the governor might well change his mind again because of recent strong data. "I suspect the Bank will ask for a 50 basis point rise after the election and that a Labour Chancellor will allow one."

Bell is forecasting that UK underlying retail price infaltion, due for release on Thursday morning, stayed at an annual rate of 3.1 percent in February, above the market consensus of a fall to 2.9 percent, and she warns there could be more falls in gilt prices if she is right.
Bell says the underlying inflation rate will stay well above the government's target of 2.5 percent unless the pound starts rising again and continues doing so.
"Remaining steady is not enough, there has to be a sustained rise to get inflation down," she said.
But HSBC markets economists are not convinced of the need for a rate rise to keep inflation in check yet.
"The inflation picture is still pretty good," said HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes.

"With consumers still behaving in a price-conscious manner, stronger high street activity will not prevent underlying inflation from falling this year as the dramatic easing in cost pressures seen in recent months feeds into the retail environment," he said.
Loynes' colleague, Dharshini David, takes heart from the improvement in British productivity also shown in today's data.
"Higher earnings growth is not inflationary if it is matched by higher productivity," she said.
UK unit labour costs growth nudged down to 3.1 percent in January from 3.4 percent in December.
But she acknowledged that unemployment data show a significant tightening in the labour market even if it is not as yet exerting strong upward pressure on inflation.
UK seasonally adjusted unemployment tumbled by 68,200 in February, well above forecasts of a 40,000 drop.
Conservative Prime Minister John Major trumpeted the fall in the jobless total as an example of the benefits of his government's policies.
The opposition Labour Party dismissed the release as "fantasy figures", saying they showed the number of people elegible for benefit payments not the number who wanted a job and could not find one.

Analysts said that the figures have been distorted downwards by the introduction of the Jobseekers allowance but even so, they say unemployment is probably falling by around 30,000 per month, twice as fast as last summer.
"We would not be surprised to see unemployment fall below 1-1/2 million by year end," HSBC's David said.
